uphill/curve: The goal is to make a function as small as possible. Here is f as a function of a single number, w, which sits at three.
uphill/slope: The gradient, g, is the slope of f right there. It is plus two: moving w to the right makes f go up.
uphill/against: So to go downhill, step the other way, against the gradient: a move of minus eta times g, where eta, the Greek letter eta, is a small positive number. w moves left, and f drops.
uphill/left: On the other side of the valley the slope is negative, so stepping against it moves w to the right. Either way, the step goes downhill.
rule/rule: That is the whole rule, written w gets w minus eta g. The arrow reads “gets”: the new w is the old w, minus eta times g.
rule/eta: Eta is the step size: a small positive number that sets how far each step goes.
rule/num: Try it where w is three and the slope g is two, with eta equal to zero point five. The step, eta times g, is one, and three minus one is two.
rule/neg: At minus one the slope is minus two, so eta times g is minus one. Subtracting a negative adds: minus one, plus one, is zero. w moves right, still downhill.
rule/steep: The step is proportional to g, so a steep slope makes a big step. From three, g goes two, one, a half: near the bottom the slope flattens, and the steps shrink on their own.
rule/vector: When w is a vector, every entry steps at once. Entry i, written w sub i with the index set low, moves against g sub i, its own entry of the gradient.
rule/vnum: With w equal to one and minus a half, g equal to two and minus one, and eta zero point one: eta times g is zero point two and minus zero point one. Subtract entry by entry, and w becomes zero point eight and minus zero point four.
drop/tangent: How much does one step lower f? Close up, the curve is almost its tangent line, so f changes by about the slope times the move.
drop/formula: The move is minus eta g. Times the slope g, that is minus eta g squared. Here, minus zero point four, and the true change is minus zero point three eight.
drop/always: Eta g squared is never negative, written eta g squared is at least zero, where the sign greater than or equal reads “is at least”. So a small enough step never raises f.
drop/sum: When w is a vector, each entry adds its own minus eta g squared. For g of two and minus one, with eta zero point one: two squared, plus minus one squared, is four plus one, five. Minus zero point one times five is minus zero point five.
